slides.title: One unit, one rule, one analyst and a week of requests
slides.text: The case One unit, one rule, one analyst and a week of requests Al-Qimam University : a fictional public university, six colleges, 18,000 students The Student Success Unit runs Awn, a rule that refers students to academic support You are Ohoud Al-Lihyani , the unit's analyst Every record is synthetic, made with a fixed seed Who Role Jassim Al-Nuaimi Director of the unit Dr. Ibtisam Al-Khayyat Vice-rector, a sponsor Dr. Nabil Al-Faraj Dean of engineering Rami Al-Tuwaijri Registrar, data owner Shatha Al-Omair Data protection officer Hazza Al-Marri Liaison of a government partner

slides.title: Awn refers a student on two signals
slides.text: The rule under study Awn refers a student on two signals Attendance recorded rate below 75% → or midterm mark below 2.5 out of 5 → Referral an advisor contacts the student 18,000 students this term 2,040 referred by Awn 2,191 ended the term struggling

slides.title: Prove your setup in two minutes

Your laptop Clone the repository, then in labs/ run uv run jupyter lab and open the same notebook. What you need. Python and pandas. No lab calls a model, needs a key or downloads anything beyond the repository.

slides.title: The pre-work gave you the instruments; this course is about using them at a desk
slides.text: Where you start The pre-work gave you the instruments; this course is about using them at a desk You know The PDPL's vocabulary, the four classification levels, the eight sharing principles, what a pseudonym does and does not hide. You practise here Testing a request, cutting an extract, classifying outputs, releasing tables, comparing groups, documenting, saying no with an alternative. Later, in DS-309 Measured re-identification risk, differential privacy, synthetic data, fairness audits of models, model cards.

slides.title: What the law asks of an analyst
slides.text: Session 1 What the law asks of an analyst Name the PDPL rules an analysis request engages, from lawful basis to transfer Distinguish analysis inside the collection purpose from a new purpose, a disclosure and a transfer Decide which requests go to the data protection officer before any data is touched 01

slides.title: Every step of an analysis is "processing" in the law
slides.text: The first idea Every step of an analysis is "processing" in the law The PDPL's definition lists collecting, storing, linking, using, disclosing, sharing, publishing and destroying A query, a join, a chart and an email attachment are each on that list The University is the controller: it sets the purpose. You act for it So the question is never "is this analysis?" but "which rules does this step engage?" At Al-Qimam Pulling 30 columns "to have a look" is collecting and storing. Joining the counselling register is linking. Sending a table to a dean is disclosing inside the controller; sending it to the Observatory is disclosing outside it.

slides.title: Four kinds of request, four gates
slides.text: Sort the request first Four kinds of request, four gates The request is The gate In the case Inside the collection purpose The purpose students were told Does Awn reach struggling students? A new internal purpose Only the cases Article 10 lists A dean wants names with counselling visits A disclosure to another entity Only the cases Article 15 lists The Observatory wants records A transfer outside the Kingdom Article 29 and the transfer regulation An upload to a notebook service abroad Method. Name the kind before you argue about the data. The kind tells you which article to open.

slides.title: A university's analysis rarely rests on consent
slides.text: Lawful basis A university's analysis rarely rests on consent Consent is the default, and Article 6 lists cases that need none An agreement the student is party to , or another law: enrolment, teaching, assessment, support Legitimate interest of the controller: never for sensitive data Advertising sent to a person needs prior consent, whatever else is true What goes wrong. "They agreed to the terms at registration" used as a basis for anything. The basis covers the purposes in the notice. A new purpose needs its own gate.

slides.title: Statistics without consent are allowed, on four duties
slides.text: The analyst's own article Statistics without consent are allowed, on four duties The law allows it when the data does not specifically identify the person, or the evidence of identity is destroyed before the data is disclosed (not for sensitive data), or another law or an agreement requires it. State the purpose in the record of processing Collect only the minimum the purpose needs Pseudonymise wherever the purpose can still be met Make sure the work has no negative impact on the people in the data

slides.title: Health data sits in three ordinary-looking columns
slides.text: Sensitive data Health data sits in three ordinary-looking columns Column Why it is health data disability_type A health condition, stated counselling_visits A health service received advisor_note Free text: surgery, treatment, a hearing aid The PDPL's sensitive kinds include health data, ethnic origin, beliefs, criminal and biometric data Health data: access for the fewest staff who need it to provide the service Legitimate interest never covers it A registered or none flag is still health data

slides.title: A student can ask what you hold, and the extract has an end date
slides.text: Rights and retention A student can ask what you hold, and the extract has an end date Rights: to be informed, to access, to get a copy, to correct, to have data destroyed when no longer needed The University answers within 30 days Retention: destroy personal data when the purpose is met; data that no longer identifies anyone may be kept What this means at your desk Know where every copy of an extract is. Give each extract a destruction date in the log. Keep the pseudonym key in the unit, so a student's rows can be found for an access request and nowhere else.

slides.title: Three words that are not synonyms: disclosure, transfer, breach
slides.text: When data leaves Three words that are not synonyms: disclosure, transfer, breach Disclosure Someone outside the controller gets access. Allowed only in listed cases, such as a public entity asking for a public-interest purpose. Transfer The data is processed outside the Kingdom. Needs an adequate level of protection or approved safeguards, and the minimum data. Breach Access nobody allowed: a lost laptop, a file sent to the wrong list. The University notifies the authority within 72 hours where harm is expected. Your part in a breach. Tell the data protection officer at once. The 72 hours run from when the University knows, and you are the University.

slides.title: The analyst prepares the decision; the data protection officer owns the hard ones
slides.text: Who decides The analyst prepares the decision; the data protection officer owns the hard ones She monitors how the law is applied and supervises impact assessments She receives data subjects' requests and reports breaches She keeps the record of processing up to date Rule of thumb Inside the collection purpose: proceed, minimise, record. Anything else (a new purpose, sensitive data, a disclosure, a transfer, advertising): to her before any data is touched, with your note attached.

slides.title: Which gate does this request pass through?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which gate does this request pass through? The alumni office asks the analyst for the grade averages of last year's graduates, to invite the top tenth to a paid executive programme run with a private partner. Which rule decides the answer? Purpose limitation is satisfied, because the data stays inside the University The sensitive-data rule, because grades are sensitive data Purpose limitation and marketing consent: a new purpose that is advertising The disclosure rule, because the alumni office is another entity

slides.title: Five requests, which rules
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min Five requests, which rules Map five requests to the PDPL principles they engage, and write the note that says so for one of them. D1_1_five_requests.ipynb Read the five requests and the privacy notice 4 min Name the kind of processing each request is 5 min Mark the rules each request engages 8 min Flag the requests that go to the data protection officer 3 min Write the note for one request 5 min ✱ Stretch: Add a sixth request: a student asks for a copy of her data used in the analysis

slides.title: Purpose, minimisation and secondary use
slides.text: Session 2 Purpose, minimisation and secondary use Write a purpose precise enough to decide each field against Cut an extract to the fields the purpose needs, keeping, coarsening or dropping each with a reason Recognise a secondary use and name what the law and the national rules require before it starts 02

slides.title: A purpose is precise enough when it can reject a column
slides.text: Purpose A purpose is precise enough when it can reject a column Too loose to decide anything "Understand student success." Every one of the 30 columns might help with that. Precise enough to cut with "Evaluate whether Awn's referrals in term 1 reached the students who ended the term struggling, by college and level, to decide whether to extend the rule." It names the decision, the population, the measure and the breakdown The law: collect for purposes directly related to the controller's own, and process only for those

slides.title: Every field gets one of three verdicts
slides.text: Minimisation Every field gets one of three verdicts Keep The purpose needs it as it is: the rule's inputs, its output, the outcome, the breakdown. Coarsen The purpose needs a rougher form: a band for a date, a flag for a grade, a pseudonym for a student number. Drop The purpose does not need it. "It might be useful" is not a need. The legal test. Content limited to the minimum necessary for the purpose, and nothing that identifies a person once the purpose is achieved.

slides.title: The Awn evaluation needs 8 of the registry's 30 columns
slides.text: From the lab's run The Awn evaluation needs 8 of the registry's 30 columns Dropped 22 Kept 7 Coarsened 1 Kept: college, level, admission route, attendance, midterm mark, referral, outcome Coarsened: the student number, into a project pseudonym Dropped: names, identity numbers, contacts, addresses, bank accounts, health fields, notes, and the exact term grade

slides.title: Pattern rules find the identifiers that have a shape, and miss the rest
slides.text: Personal data detection Pattern rules find the identifiers that have a shape, and miss the rest In 2,400 advisor notes Notes Found by a pattern? A mobile number 180 Yes An identity number 70 Yes A health remark 210 No Another student's name 80 No re.search(r"\b05\d{8}\b", note) # phone re.search(r"\b[12]\d{9}\b", note) # identity So. A free-text column is dropped whole, not cleaned. Detection tools (regular expressions, Presidio) lower the risk; they do not certify a text.

slides.title: "Anonymised" has a legal meaning, and your extract does not meet it
slides.text: A word used loosely "Anonymised" has a legal meaning, and your extract does not meet it Pseudonymised Identifiers replaced by a code. Someone holds the key, and each row is still one student. Still personal data. Every rule still applies. Anonymised Re-identification is impossible, the controller has assessed that, and keeps assessing it as methods change. Only then is it no longer personal data. At your desk. Say "pseudonymised extract". Use a keyed hash with a key for this project only, so two extracts cannot be joined.

slides.title: A new purpose for old data is a new decision
slides.text: Secondary use A new purpose for old data is a new decision Secondary use: using data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for The PDPL allows it only in listed cases: consent, a public entity acting in the public interest, data that no longer identifies anyone, and a few more The General Rules for Secondary Use of Data govern requests between entities for the public interest or for research What the Rules ask of an applicant A legitimate purpose that is not profit-seeking. Only the minimum data for it. A request to the entity that is the source of the data, or proof of its approval. A rejection must give its reasons.

slides.title: The cut is a decision, so it leaves a log
slides.text: Recording why The cut is a decision, so it leaves a log Field Decision Reason student_id coarsen A project pseudonym keeps one row per student without the registry number admission_route keep Bridging-year entrants have no midterm mark; needed to read the rule's result term_gpa drop The outcome flag already says struggled or not advisor_note drop Free text: cannot be checked field by field Who reads it. The data owner who approves the extract, the reviewer who audits it, and you, six months later.

slides.title: Which extract fits the purpose?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which extract fits the purpose? Purpose: "report the share of first-year students who end the term struggling, by college". Which extract is the minimum that serves it? A pseudonym, the college, the level and the outcome flag, for first-year students The same, plus the student number and email in case a college wants to follow up The college, the level, the exact term grade and the date of birth The college, the level and the outcome flag for all 18,000 students, filtered later

slides.title: Cut the extract
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min Cut the extract Cut an extract to the fields the purpose needs, recording why, and find the identifiers hiding in free text. D1_2_cut_extract.ipynb Read the purpose and the 30 columns of the registry 3 min Decide keep, coarsen or drop for each field, with a reason 8 min Scan the advisor notes for identifiers with rules 5 min Build the extract with a project pseudonym 6 min Write the minimisation log 3 min ✱ Stretch: Decide the fields again for a second purpose, the partner's study, and say what makes it a secondary use

slides.title: Classifying data and outputs
slides.text: Session 3 Classifying data and outputs Classify a dataset or an output with the impact questions of the Data Classification Policy Apply the highest-level rule to combined data and say when an aggregate can be Public Name the control each level requires, including what may be entered into an AI tool 03

slides.title: A table, a chart and a list are data, and each needs a level
slides.text: The idea of this session A table, a chart and a list are data, and each needs a level The policy covers all data a public entity receives, produces or manages, in any form An output does not inherit the level of its source Classify when you create it: until someone does, it is treated as Restricted In the Awn evaluation One Restricted registry produces a Restricted extract, a Restricted worklist, a Restricted draft table and, after approval, a Public table of referral rates by college.

slides.title: The level follows the impact of disclosure
slides.text: Recap from the pre-work The level follows the impact of disclosure Level Impact What it looks like at a university Top Secret High Not in a student-success unit Secret Medium Not in a student-success unit Restricted Low Student records, the extract, a named worklist, a draft with small cells Public None The timetable, a released table of rates by college Why not Secret? The policy rates the disclosure of an individual's personal information as a low impact. Low impact leads to Restricted or Public.

slides.title: Low impact needs two more questions
slides.text: Restricted or Public? Low impact needs two more questions Impact is low harm to individuals is limited and short-term → Would disclosure conflict with a law? Yes: Restricted → Do the benefits of openness outweigh the harm? Yes: Public. No: Restricted The extract Rows about single students. Disclosure would break the PDPL. Restricted at the first question. Rates by college Nobody is identified, no law is broken, publishing helps students and the public. Public.

slides.title: A joined file takes the highest level of its parts
slides.text: Combined data A joined file takes the highest level of its parts Timetable Public ↓ joined to the registry Restricted ↓ Attendance by time of day, per student Restricted The policy's fourth principle: the highest level of protection for an integrated dataset The reverse also happens: an aggregate of Restricted rows can be Public So the level is set for each output, by what that output would reveal

slides.title: The level tells you how to mark, open, store, send and end the data
slides.text: Controls The level tells you how to mark, open, store, send and end the data Control Restricted item Public item Protective marking Marked on the file and in the email None needed Access Need to know, least privilege Open Storage Not left unattended; encrypted Anywhere Sharing An agreed secure channel Any channel Retention and disposal On the schedule, disposal logged On the schedule Before release Second-person check, owner's approval Done

slides.title: Only Public data goes into a generative AI tool
slides.text: What may go into AI tools Only Public data goes into a generative AI tool AnalystHere are 200 rows of the extract. Summarise the patterns by college. Hosted assistantHappy to help. I have stored your file... Government employees enter nothing classified Restricted or higher, and nothing unclassified A pseudonymised extract is Restricted: no A released table of rates: yes Asking for code without pasting data: yes

slides.title: You propose a level; the data owner classifies; a reviewer checks
slides.text: Roles and time You propose a level; the data owner classifies; a reviewer checks Analyst proposes a level and controls for each output → Data owner (the registrar) classifies → Reviewer in the data management office checks within a month Levels change. Set the trigger when you classify: "Restricted until the release is approved", "Public from the publication date". Record it in the register.

slides.title: What level is this output today?
slides.text: Checkpoint What level is this output today? You compute a table of registered-disability counts by college and nationality group from the pseudonymised extract. Two cells are under 10 and one is 1. Nobody has reviewed it. What is its level now? Public, because it is an aggregate with no names Restricted, because every output of a Restricted source stays Restricted Secret, because it contains health data Restricted, because a cell of 1 can single out a student, until it is suppressed and checked

slides.title: Classify and control
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min Classify and control Classify four datasets and three outputs and name each control. D1_3_classify_control.ipynb Run the impact questions on the four datasets 7 min Classify the three outputs 6 min Apply the highest-level rule to a joined file 3 min Name the controls for each item 6 min Decide what may be entered into an AI tool 3 min ✱ Stretch: Set a declassification trigger for the referral table and say who approves it

slides.title: Sharing requests
slides.text: Session 4 Sharing requests Assess a sharing request against the tests of the Data Sharing Policy and the rules for secondary use Choose the form of release: record level, pseudonymised or aggregate Draft approval conditions under the policy's control headings and name who signs 04

slides.title: The policy expects you to share, and tells you how
slides.text: The starting point The policy expects you to share, and tells you how Its first principle is a data sharing culture: entities share what they produce The other seven principles are the conditions: legitimate purpose, authorised access, transparency, accountability, security, ethical use, one source of truth For personal data the PDPL's disclosure cases apply on top The analyst's part You will be the person who knows what the data contains. You prepare the assessment and the conditions. The data management office decides, with the data protection officer.

slides.title: A request has three roles and one front door
slides.text: Parties and route A request has three roles and one front door Role In the case Data requester Masarat Labour Market Observatory Data sharing entity Al-Qimam University Data source entity The University for marks; another entity for identity numbers The front door is the data management office, never an analyst's inbox Requests for analytical purposes go to the National Data Bank first Between government entities: the controls template. With a private entity: a data sharing agreement

slides.title: Three tests decide whether sharing can go ahead
slides.text: The assessment Three tests decide whether sharing can go ahead 1 · Legitimate purpose A legal basis or a justified operational need. For the Observatory: its mandate, a public-interest purpose. Met. 2 · Minimum data Only what the purpose needs. It asked for 11 fields of all 18,000 students. Not met. 3 · The source's consent Needed for fields the University is not the source of. Met with conditions. Time. The office assesses within 10 business days and gives its reasons in writing. A rejected request may be corrected and sent again.

slides.title: Choose the least revealing form that still serves the purpose
slides.text: In what form Choose the least revealing form that still serves the purpose Form What leaves Serves a linkage study? Aggregate Counts and averages by programme No Pseudonymised Rows under a code only the University can reverse No Record level, minimised Rows with the identity number and the few fields needed Yes 11 × 18,000 fields and students asked for 5 × 3,612 offered: final-year students, five fields

slides.title: Eight headings turn "yes, but" into something signable
slides.text: The conditions Eight headings turn "yes, but" into something signable Legal basis: the purpose, and no other use Authorisation: named people, need to know Data type: the fields, the format, the detail Pre-processing: masking, aggregation before or after Sharing means: the channel; retention and destruction Usage and protection: the level, limits, onward use Duration and termination: end date, what happens then Liability: who answers for what Read the request for its weak points. "By email", "and its contractors", "a consulting firm", "kept for future studies": each one becomes a condition.

slides.title: The level of the data decides who signs
slides.text: The decision record The level of the data decides who signs Level of the shared data Who signs for the sharing entity Secret, Top Secret The head of the entity or a delegate Restricted The director of the data management office Public No assessment or agreement needed The record names the decision, the level, the signatory and who was consulted It goes into the record of processing and the office's log of requests Sharing records are kept for five years after the request ends

slides.title: Change one fact and the decision changes with it
slides.text: Decisions move Change one fact and the decision changes with it If the request changed to What now applies A private company as requester A data sharing agreement, a licence under the secondary-use rules, no profit-seeking purpose, and a different PDPL disclosure case Analysts outside the Kingdom The transfer rules: adequate protection or approved safeguards Disability status added Sensitive data: the narrowest reading of every test Aggregates only Small-cell rules, and perhaps a Public table In the capstone. The assessor changes one fact of your partner's request and you revise the decision aloud.

slides.title: What is the right first answer to this request?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is the right first answer to this request? A government health authority emails the analyst: "For a wellbeing study, send names and counselling visit counts of all students." What comes first? Send it: a public entity asked, for the public interest Forward it to the data management office and the data protection officer, with your assessment Refuse: counselling data is health data and is never shared Send pseudonymised rows instead, which removes the names

slides.title: The Observatory's request
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min The Observatory's request Assess a partner's sharing request and draft the approval conditions. D1_4_sharing_request.ipynb Read the request and name the parties and the route 4 min Assess it against the three tests 6 min Choose the form of release 5 min Draft the conditions under the eight control headings 7 min Fill the decision record and name who signs 3 min ✱ Stretch: The partner adds a consultant outside the Kingdom: revise the decision

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 1 Three things to keep Name the kind first Inside the purpose, a new purpose, a disclosure, a transfer. The kind tells you which rule to open and who decides. The purpose cuts the data Keep, coarsen or drop, with a reason in a log. Thirty columns became eight. Outputs get a level and requests get conditions Classify what you produce. Answer a partner with a form of release and eight conditions.

slides.title: Day 2: fair and safe outputs
slides.text: Tomorrow Day 2: fair and safe outputs A table that looks harmless and points at one student. A rule that looks neutral and is wrong more often for two groups. Bring: your setup, working Recall: a confidence interval for a proportion

slides.title: Fair and safe outputs
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work Fair and safe outputs Day 2: Release tables that single nobody out, and compare groups with honest uncertainty Data Science Track3 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-207

slides.title: Fair and safe outputs
slides.text: Today Fair and safe outputs Session 1 · Aggregate release and small cells An aggregate table can still point at one student Session 2 · Where bias enters Bias enters in recording, coverage, labels and use, before any metric Session 3 · Comparing groups Referral and error rates by group, each with its interval Session 4 · Naming the bias Two candidate bias types for a gap, and the check that separates them

slides.title: Which statement about the pseudonymised extract is right?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which statement about the pseudonymised extract is right? The analysis extract has 13 columns per student under a project pseudonym, with no names or identity numbers. A colleague wants to paste 500 rows into a hosted AI assistant to get plotting code. Fine: without names the rows are anonymous Not allowed: the extract is personal data classified Restricted; describe the columns and ask for code Fine if the assistant's history is switched off Not allowed: student data is classified Secret

slides.title: The group comparison is a separate decision, already approved and logged
slides.text: Where today starts The group comparison is a separate decision, already approved and logged Yesterday's extract dropped gender, nationality and disability status: its purpose did not need them Checking the rule's errors by group does need them Disability status is health data, so the data protection officer decided Log entry L002, approved by Shatha Al-Omair Gender, nationality group, disability status and remote accommodation are added to the extract for the group comparison. It runs only on the pseudonymised extract inside the unit and is reported in aggregate.

slides.title: Aggregate release and small cells
slides.text: Session 1 Aggregate release and small cells Explain how a small cell, a total or a second release singles out a student Apply a threshold rule with complementary suppression and log each suppressed cell Test a release for recovery by subtraction and by differencing before it leaves 01

slides.title: An aggregate table can point at one student in three ways
slides.text: The idea of this session An aggregate table can point at one student in three ways A small cell A count of 1 in "Computing, non-Saudi, registered disability" is a person, to anyone who knows that college. A total Hide the 1 and print the row total: the reader subtracts and has it back. A second table Two tables that each look safe differ by exactly the students one of them leaves out. Singling out means a reader can tell that a cell is one particular person, and so learns what the table says about that person.

slides.title: A threshold rule: no count from 1 to 9 leaves the unit
slides.text: The rule A threshold rule: no count from 1 to 9 leaves the unit The unit's release policy sets 10. It is the University's own choice No national instrument sets a number. The national guideline requires that aggregated data cannot be used to identify a person Practice elsewhere: 3 as an absolute floor, 5 or 10 as common minimums Choosing a threshold Higher when the attribute is sensitive (health), when the population is small and people know each other (a college), and when more tables on the same population will follow.

slides.title: The draft: students with a registered disability, by college and nationality group
slides.text: From the lab's run The draft: students with a registered disability, by college and nationality group College Saudi non-Saudi Total Arts and Humanities 65 8 73 Business 92 8 100 Computing 54 1 55 Engineering 81 12 93 Health Sciences 51 3 54 Science 50 4 54 5 cells from 1 to 9 One student. The cell of 1 states a health fact about a person a whole college can name.

slides.title: Suppress the small cells, keep the totals, and all five come back
slides.text: Attack one Suppress the small cells, keep the totals, and all five come back College Saudi non-Saudi Total Arts and Humanities 65 c 73 Business 92 c 100 Computing 54 c 55 Engineering 81 12 93 Health Sciences 51 c 54 Science 50 c 54 55 - 54 # Computing, non-Saudi: 1 54 - 51 # Health Sciences: 3 What changed. How the table looks. Not what it reveals.

slides.title: Complementary suppression protects the cell and can eat the table
slides.text: The repair, and its price Complementary suppression protects the cell and can eat the table Where one hidden cell can be subtracted back, hide a second cell in the same row and column Repeat until no row or column has exactly one hidden cell In the draft: 10 of 12 cells end up hidden, including counts of 50 to 92 nobody needed to hide Redesign beats repair Two one-way tables: by college (54 to 100) and by nationality group (393 and 36). Every cell is 10 or more, no suppression, and almost the same message.

slides.title: Two safe tables can differ by one student
slides.text: Attack two Two safe tables can differ by one student Registered disability Published last month, all Asked for now, Saudi only Difference Arts and Humanities 73 65 8 Business 100 92 8 Computing 55 54 1 Health Sciences 54 51 3 Science 54 50 4 Each table passes the threshold alone: every count is 50 or more The difference is the group the second table left out The check: before a release, compare it with every earlier table on the same population

slides.title: Suppression is one of four tools
slides.text: Beyond suppression Suppression is one of four tools Method What it does What the reader loses Coarsen the categories Merge colleges, or nationalities into two groups Detail; usually the cheapest loss Suppress Hide small cells and their complements Cells, sometimes most of them Round or band Counts to a base of 5; "fewer than 10" Exactness of every cell Perturb Small random changes to counts Trust that a number is the number Later. Noise with a mathematical guarantee (differential privacy) and measured re-identification risk are in DS-309.

slides.title: A cell of zero or of everyone can disclose too
slides.text: Not only small counts A cell of zero or of everyone can disclose too Everyone in a group "All 14 students of programme X were referred." No small cell, and you now know the referral status of each of the 14. Nobody in a group "0 of 14 were not referred" is the same sentence. A zero that tells you about everyone else is not harmless. Check rates of 0% and 100% in small groups as well as counts The unit's rule covers counts of 1 to 9; this case needs your judgement and a line in the log

slides.title: Every suppressed cell has a line in the log, and every release a line in the register
slides.text: The evidence Every suppressed cell has a line in the log, and every release a line in the register Table Row Column Kind Reason T3 Computing non-Saudi primary count of 1 to 9 T3 Computing Saudi complementary protects a suppressed cell from subtraction Saudi-only by college all all not released differencing against the release of 2026-10 reveals counts of 1 to 9 Second person. The unit's policy: a table with a suppressed cell is checked by someone who did not make it, before it is proposed as Public.

slides.title: Is this table ready for release?
slides.text: Checkpoint Is this table ready for release? A table of referred students by college and level has one cell of 4. The analyst replaces it with "c" and keeps the row and column totals. The threshold is 10. What is the state of the table? Ready: the only small cell is suppressed Not ready: all totals must be removed from every table Ready, provided the cell is shown as "fewer than 10" Not ready: the 4 is recovered from its row total until a second cell in that row and column is suppressed

slides.title: Suppress, then attack
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · 25 min Suppress, then attack Apply a threshold rule and test for singling out by differencing. D2_1_small_cells.ipynb Count the cells under the threshold in three draft tables 4 min Suppress them and log each cell with its reason 6 min Recover a suppressed cell from the totals 4 min Add complementary suppression and test again 6 min Difference the table against an earlier release 5 min ✱ Stretch: Round the counts to a base of 5 in place of suppression and compare what a reader loses

slides.title: Where bias enters
slides.text: Session 2 Where bias enters Trace a rule's data from the event to the decision and mark where bias can enter Distinguish a recording problem, a coverage problem, a label problem and a use problem Measure one entry point with data instead of arguing about it 02

slides.title: Bias is a systematic error that falls on some groups more than others
slides.text: A working definition Bias is a systematic error that falls on some groups more than others It needs no intent: a process that records or covers people unequally is enough It is not noise: more data of the same kind does not remove it It enters before any metric is computed The national frame Fairness is the first of SDAIA's AI Ethics Principles: act to eliminate bias in the data, the design and the use of a system. The AI Bias Reference Guide names more than a hundred types, with how each arises and how to mitigate it.

slides.title: Awn's data passes six stages, and each is an entry point
slides.text: Walk the path Awn's data passes six stages, and each is an entry point 1 · Recording A card read at the door of a teaching room 2 · Marks Midterm marks entered in the registry 3 · Thresholds 75% and 2.5, set in 2023 on two colleges 4 · Outcome label "Struggled": a term average below 2.5 5 · Use An advisor contacts the referred student 6 · Reporting One rate for the whole University The question at each stage. For whom could this step go wrong more often than for others?

slides.title: The card record is 17 points too low for students who attend remotely
slides.text: Entry point 1, measured The card record is 17 points too low for students who attend remotely Remote accommodation 16.8 points Other students -0.1 points Roll call minus card record, from an audit of 1,600 students Of 300 students with a remote accommodation, 191 are below the 75% limit on the card record On the roll call, 14 are

slides.title: Over a third of non-Saudi students have no midterm mark in the registry
slides.text: Entry point 2, measured Over a third of non-Saudi students have no midterm mark in the registry Non-Saudi students 36.2% Saudi students 3.4% 1,244 students have no mark; every one is a bridging-year entrant Their marks are in the bridging programme's own system For them, half of the rule cannot fire Where you see it is not where it comes from. The effect appears under nationality; the cause is the admission route.

slides.title: Thresholds carry their history, and labels carry a definition
slides.text: Entry points 3 and 4 Thresholds carry their history, and labels carry a definition Thresholds from 2023, two colleges A limit tuned on Business and Engineering may not fit Health Sciences, where one student in five ends the term struggling. Past conditions built into today's rule: the guide's historical bias. "Struggled" is a choice A term average below 2.5. A student who withdraws after two courses keeps a good average and counts as "ok". Change the label and every error rate changes with it. What goes wrong. Treating the outcome column as the truth. It is one more measurement, with its own blind spots.

slides.title: What happens after the referral changes what the data says about it
slides.text: Entry points 5 and 6 What happens after the referral changes what the data says about it Support that works hides itself. A referred student who is helped and passes counts as a referral that was "not needed" Take-up differs. Who answers an advisor's call, who can come during working hours? One number for everyone hides a rule that fails a small group The loop If next year's thresholds are tuned on this year's outcomes, colleges with good advisors will look as if they need fewer referrals. The guide's feedback loop bias.

slides.title: An entry point is a hypothesis until someone measures it
slides.text: Method An entry point is a hypothesis until someone measures it An opinion "Attendance data is probably unfair to some students." Nobody can act on it, and nobody can refute it. A measurement "For 300 students with a remote accommodation the record is 17 points below the roll call; 191 fall under the limit on paper, 14 in fact." A size, a group, a consequence. The audit sampled all 300 students of the small group and 1,300 others at random: a small group needs all its members to be measured at all

slides.title: Where did the bias enter?
slides.text: Checkpoint Where did the bias enter? A library fines late returns. Evening students are fined twice as often. A return is logged when staff scan the book; the desk closes before evening classes end, and the drop box is scanned the next morning. Where does the gap come from? Recording: the return time is logged later than the true return for one group Outcome: evening students return books later Thresholds: the loan period is too short for evening students Reporting: the fine rate is reported for all students together

slides.title: Four entry points
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · 25 min Four entry points Mark four points where bias can enter the referral data, and measure two of them. D2_2_bias_entry_points.ipynb Trace Awn's data from the event to the referral 5 min Mark four points where bias can enter 8 min Measure the attendance record against the roll-call audit 6 min Measure missing midterm marks by group 4 min Rank which entry point to check first 2 min ✱ Stretch: Find a fifth entry point after the referral: who takes up the support that is offered

slides.title: Comparing groups
slides.text: Session 3 Comparing groups Compute referral, false-referral and missed-student rates by group Report each rate and each difference with a confidence interval Check whether a gap survives inside colleges before explaining it 03

slides.title: One rule, four outcomes, three rates
slides.text: What to compare One rule, four outcomes, three rates Struggled Did not struggle Referred caught: 1,209 false referral: 831 Not referred missed: 982 left alone: 14,978 Referral rate = referred / all = 11.3% False-referral rate = false referrals / did not struggle = 5.3% Missed rate = missed / struggled = 44.8% Not "accuracy". Awn is right for 90% of students, and misses 45% of those it exists for.

slides.title: The two errors hurt different students in different ways
slides.text: Why two error rates The two errors hurt different students in different ways A false referral A student who was fine is contacted, labelled "at risk" in a system, and takes an advisor's hour from someone else. Mild once; not mild if the label travels. A miss A student who is struggling hears from nobody. The rule existed for this student. A group can be worse off in one error and not the other, so one combined number hides it The ethics principles ask that metrics be chosen by the effect of the decision and the harm of each kind of error

slides.title: A rate without its interval hides how many students it rests on
slides.text: Uncertainty A rate without its interval hides how many students it rests on Missed rate Struggling students Rate (95% interval) Saudi 1,971 42.9% (40.8 to 45.1) non-Saudi 220 61.8% (55.2 to 68.0) Registered disability 61 13.1% (6.8 to 23.8) The denominator of a missed rate is the struggling students of the group, not the group Use the Wilson interval: it behaves for small counts and rates near 0 or 1 For a difference, an interval on the difference itself

slides.title: Two groups stand out, in two different errors
slides.text: From the lab's run Two groups stand out, in two different errors Group Students Referral rate False-referral rate Missed rate Women 8,218 12.3% 5.5% 43.2% Men 9,782 10.5% 5.1% 46.4% Saudi 16,063 11.8% 5.4% 42.9% non-Saudi 1,937 7.8% 3.9% 61.8% No registered disability 17,571 10.6% 4.6% 45.7% Registered disability 429 41.7% 34.2% 13.1%

slides.title: Report every comparison you made, with its interval
slides.text: Differences Report every comparison you made, with its interval Comparison Rate Difference 95% interval Reading Registered disability minus none false referral +29.7 points +25.0 to +34.7 clear non-Saudi minus Saudi missed +18.9 points +12.0 to +25.4 clear Women minus men referral +1.9 points +0.9 to +2.8 clear, see next slide First generation minus not missed +1.1 points -3.3 to +5.6 could be zero First generation minus not false referral +0.6 points -0.2 to +1.4 could be zero The two rows at the bottom belong in the report. Leaving out comparisons that found nothing makes the others look selected.

slides.title: The gender gap vanishes inside every college
slides.text: Before explaining a gap The gender gap vanishes inside every college College Share of women Referral rate Women minus men (95% interval) Health Sciences 76% 20.0% -1.2 points (-5.1 to +2.5) Science 59% 14.4% -1.1 points (-3.9 to +1.6) Arts and Humanities 50% 10.6% +0.3 points (-1.9 to +2.5) Business 39% 7.8% -0.8 points (-2.5 to +1.0) Computing 37% 9.0% 0.0 points (-2.3 to +2.4) Engineering 25% 9.2% -0.3 points (-2.3 to +2.0) Overall: +1.9 points. Women study more often in the colleges where everyone is referred more. The rule treats women and men in the same college alike.

slides.title: A library computes the rates; you choose the comparisons
slides.text: Tools A library computes the rates; you choose the comparisons g = df.groupby("nationality_group") missed = g.apply(lambda d: (~d.referred & d.struggled).sum() / d.struggled.sum()) Grouped metrics in pandas or SQL: a group-by and three ratios A fairness library (Fairlearn's MetricFrame): the same table in one call, for many metrics Neither chooses the groups, the strata, the intervals or the question Small groups twice. A rate on 8 students is too uncertain to interpret and too small to publish. Both rules apply.

slides.title: What can the analyst claim?
slides.text: Checkpoint What can the analyst claim? Awn missed 8 of 61 struggling students with a registered disability (13%, interval 7% to 24%) and 974 of 2,130 others (46%, interval 44% to 48%). Which sentence is supported? The rule works better for students with a registered disability Nothing can be said: 61 students are too few Fewer of this group were missed, by an uncertain margin; read the false-referral rate beside it The rule is biased in favour of students with a registered disability

slides.text: Lab 2.3 · 25 min Rates with intervals Compare referral and error rates by group with intervals. D2_3_group_rates.ipynb Build the four outcome counts by group 5 min Compute the three rates with Wilson intervals 8 min Compute the differences with their intervals 5 min Check the gender gap inside each college 5 min Write the result in one sentence per gap 2 min ✱ Stretch: Compute the rates for one intersection of two groups and say what the interval allows you to claim

slides.title: Naming the bias
slides.text: Session 4 Naming the bias Match an observed gap to candidate bias types in the AI Bias Reference Guide Design the check that separates two candidate causes State what a fairness metric cannot settle and who decides the rest 04

slides.title: A gap is an observation; a bias type is an explanation
slides.text: The idea of this session A gap is an observation; a bias type is an explanation 1 · Observe a gap with its interval → 2 · Name two candidates that would need different fixes → 3 · Design a check on which they disagree → 4 · Run it and say what stays open What goes wrong. Naming the first bias type that fits and stopping. One gap usually fits several names, and each name points to a different repair.

slides.title: The AI Bias Reference Guide gives each type a definition, an example and a mitigation
slides.text: The national reference The AI Bias Reference Guide gives each type a definition, an example and a mitigation Type In one line (our wording) Measurement bias Recorded values are systematically too high or too low Coverage bias The data does not adequately represent part of the population Aggregation bias Groups that differ are combined; the result fits the largest Historical bias Past assumptions or conditions no longer fit the present Feedback loop bias Outputs return as inputs and magnify an early skew Automation bias People favour a system's output over other evidence

slides.title: Is the record wrong, or does one limit not fit?
slides.text: Gap A · false referrals, registered disability Is the record wrong, or does one limit not fit? Measurement bias Attendance is recorded too low for these students. Prediction: the record is far below the roll call, and the gap is confined to students with a remote accommodation. Fix the record. Aggregation bias Attendance is recorded correctly and one limit of 75% does not fit this group. Prediction: record matches roll call, and the gap covers all students with a registered disability. Fix the rule. The check. Roll call against record, and the false-referral rate with and without a remote accommodation.

slides.title: The gap is confined to students whose attendance is under-recorded
slides.text: Gap A · the check's result The gap is confined to students whose attendance is under-recorded Registered, remote accommodation 59.4% Registered, no remote accommodation 3.6% No registered disability 4.6% False-referral rates, Lab 2.4 Intervals: 52.5 to 65.9; 1.7 to 7.7; 4.2 to 4.9 The record is 16.8 points below the roll call for the first group Measurement bias. Fix the feed of remote attendance

slides.title: Compare like with like and the gap moves to where the marks are missing
slides.text: Gap B · missed students, non-Saudi Compare like with like and the gap moves to where the marks are missing Missed rate Saudi non-Saudi Mark present 41.6% (39.4 to 43.9) 45.9% (37.6 to 54.3) Mark missing 76.7% (65.8 to 84.9) 86.2% (77.4 to 91.9) Candidates: coverage bias (no marks) or aggregation bias (limits that do not fit) With a mark, both groups are missed at similar rates Without one, both are missed three times in four or more Coverage bias. Bring the bridging programme's marks into the registry

slides.title: The name decides the fix, and a wrong name produces a harmful one
slides.text: Why the name matters The name decides the fix, and a wrong name produces a harmful one If you had concluded You would have And then "The limit does not fit students with a disability" Lowered their attendance limit Missed those who truly stop attending, and left the record wrong "The rule does not fit non-Saudi students" Set separate limits by nationality Treated students by a protected characteristic, and still missed Saudi bridging-year entrants Measurement and coverage Repaired two data feeds Fixed it for everyone the feeds had failed

slides.title: A fairness metric cannot tell you which fairness to want
slides.text: The limit of the numbers A fairness metric cannot tell you which fairness to want When groups differ in how often the outcome occurs, a rule cannot equalise every error rate and every hit rate at once Lowering false referrals for a group raises its misses, or the reverse How large a remaining gap is acceptable is not a statistical question Who decides The director of the unit owns the rule; the data protection officer owns the impact on students. You bring the rates, the intervals, the cause you could establish and what stays open. They choose.

slides.title: Which check separates the two candidates?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which check separates the two candidates? A training centre flags trainees with fewer than three logged sessions a week. One branch is flagged three times as often. Either its sessions are logged too low (measurement), or one limit does not fit a branch with fewer, longer sessions (aggregation). Which check separates the two? Recompute the flag rates with confidence intervals Compare logged sessions with the branch's attendance sheets Lower the limit for that branch and see whether the gap closes Ask the branch's trainers whether the rule seems fair

slides.title: Two gaps, two names
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · 25 min Two gaps, two names Match two observed gaps to bias types in the national guide and run the check that separates them. D2_4_name_the_bias.ipynb Read the two gaps and their intervals 3 min Pick two candidate bias types for each gap 6 min Design the check that separates them 6 min Run the two checks 7 min Record the conclusion and what stays open 3 min ✱ Stretch: Change the rule to equalise false referrals and report what happens to missed students

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 2 Three things to keep Attack your own table Small cells, then totals, then earlier releases. When suppression eats the table, redesign it. Rates by group, with intervals Referral, false referral, missed. Every comparison reported, each inside the strata that matter. Two candidates and a check A gap is not a cause. The name decides the fix, so earn the name.

slides.title: Day 3: professional conduct
slides.text: Tomorrow Day 3: professional conduct The work so far lives in your head and your notebook. Tomorrow it becomes something others can check, and you hold three conversations. You will role-play in threes: analyst, sponsor, observer No AI assistant in the role-plays

slides.title: Professional conduct
slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Responsible Data Practice and Conduct in Analytical Work Professional conduct Day 3: Document the work so others can check it, and hold the three conversations Data Science Track3 teaching days + capstone day4 sessions · 4 labsDS-207

slides.title: Professional conduct
slides.text: Today Professional conduct Session 1 · Datasheets and analysis logs A reviewer must be able to trace a number to data, decisions and approvals Session 2 · Scoping with a sponsor A vague request becomes a decision, a population, a measure and a criterion Session 3 · Pushing back without obstructing Name the harm and the rule, offer an alternative, escalate when needed Session 4 · Explaining limits Say what the result does not show and what it must not be used for

slides.title: What is the right next step?
slides.text: Review of Day 2 What is the right next step? A rule misses struggling non-Saudi students more often than Saudi students: 62% against 43%, and the interval of the difference excludes zero. What does the analyst do next? Propose a lower threshold for non-Saudi students Report that the rule discriminates by nationality Name two candidate causes and run the check on which they disagree Leave the breakdown by nationality out of the report

slides.title: Datasheets and analysis logs
slides.text: Session 1 Datasheets and analysis logs Fill a datasheet that states what the data is, how it was collected and what it must not be used for Keep an analysis log in which every decision has a reason, a date and an approver Tie a release to a version so a result can be traced and rerun 01

slides.title: "Where does the 55% come from?" must have an answer without you in the room
slides.text: The test of documentation "Where does the 55% come from?" must have an answer without you in the room The number 55% of struggling students referred → The release version, date, file fingerprints → The data a datasheet: what it is, what is wrong with it → The decisions a log: reason, date, approver The reader. A reviewer in six months, the data protection officer in an audit, your successor, and you.

slides.title: A datasheet answers what a careful user would ask before using the data
slides.text: The datasheet A datasheet answers what a careful user would ask before using the data Section The question Motivation Why was it made, for whom, for which decision? Composition What is one row? What is personal, sensitive, missing, and for whom? Collection Where does each field come from? What is recorded badly? Preprocessing What was dropped, coarsened, pseudonymised? Uses What is the approved use? What must it not be used for? Distribution Who may see it? What level? May it leave? Maintenance Who owns it? Kept until when? How is an error reported?

slides.title: A datasheet that states the data's weakness protects the analysis
slides.text: Honesty in the datasheet A datasheet that states the data's weakness protects the analysis Collection, as written in the lab "Known to be recorded badly: attendance is about 17 points too low for the 300 students with a remote accommodation, because remote sessions leave no card reading." Composition, as written in the lab "The midterm mark is missing for 1,244 students, all bridging-year entrants." A reader who finds the weakness alone stops trusting everything A reader who is told can weigh the results that depend on it

slides.title: Every decision has a reason, a date and an approver
slides.text: The analysis log Every decision has a reason, a date and an approver Id Decision Approver L001 Evaluate Awn on a pseudonymised extract of 13 fields Registrar (data owner) L002 Add four group fields for the comparison Data protection officer L003 Release two one-way tables, not the cross table Registrar; suppression checked by the director L004 Do not release the Saudi-only table by college Registrar L005 Report bridging-year entrants and remote accommodation separately Director of the unit Six fields per entry. Id, date, decision, reason, approver, where the evidence is.

slides.title: An approver is a named person with the authority to approve that thing
slides.text: Accountability An approver is a named person with the authority to approve that thing The data owner Approves extracts and releases of the data he is responsible for. Here: the registrar. The data protection officer Decides on sensitive fields, new purposes, disclosures and transfers. The owner of the decision Approves how results are reported and used. Here: the director of the unit. What goes wrong. "Approved by the team." A team cannot be asked a question in an audit, and cannot be shown to have had the authority.

slides.title: A release is a version, a date, fingerprints and one line of warning
slides.text: Decision records and versioned releases A release is a version, a date, fingerprints and one line of warning {"version": "2026.11.1", "table": "Referral rate by college", "files": {"analysis_extract.csv": "2d9ebc9f490e9f0d"}, "log_entries": ["L001", "L002", "L003"], "approved_by": "the registrar", "must_not_be_used_for": "ranking colleges or judging advisors"} A fingerprint (a hash of the file) changes if one byte changes: a version number is a claim, a fingerprint is a check A decision record keeps the options that were rejected, and why Templates live in Git beside the code, as Markdown or Quarto documents

slides.title: Some of this record is required
slides.text: Not only good practice Some of this record is required The University keeps a record of processing: the purpose, the categories of people, who the data is disclosed to, transfers, the retention period For statistics without consent, the purpose is stated in that record Sharing requests and their documents are kept for five years Disposal of data is logged Your log feeds theirs The data protection officer keeps the record of processing. An analysis log with purposes, approvals and end dates is what lets her keep it true.

slides.title: Five questions your documents must answer alone
slides.text: The peer audit Five questions your documents must answer alone Which file and which version produced the referral table released in November? Who approved the use of disability status in the group comparison, and on what condition? Why are bridging-year entrants reported separately? What must the group comparison not be used for? How many cells were suppressed in the release, and who checked the suppression? The rule of the swap. Your peer reads only your documents. No asking, no notebook.

slides.title: Which log entry would survive an audit?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which log entry would survive an audit? The analyst decided to merge two small nationality groups in a published table. Which entry lets a reviewer trace that decision? "2026-11-09. Merged groups X and Y in table T1: both had cells under 10. Approved by the registrar (data owner). Evidence: suppression log." "Merged some categories in T1 for privacy reasons. Approved." A comment in the notebook cell that does the merge "2026-11-09. Merged X and Y in T1. Decided by the analyst."

slides.title: Datasheet and log
slides.text: Lab 3.1 · 25 min Datasheet and log Fill a datasheet and log three decisions with their approver, then let a peer audit them. D3_1_datasheet_log.ipynb Fill the datasheet from the data and the notice 8 min Log three decisions with reason, date and approver 6 min Tag the release with its file fingerprints 4 min Swap with a peer and answer five audit questions 5 min Fix what the peer could not answer 2 min ✱ Stretch: Add a decision record for the choice of threshold, with the options that were rejected

slides.title: Scoping with a sponsor
slides.text: Session 2 Scoping with a sponsor Ask the questions that turn a request into a decision, a population, a measure and a time frame Agree success criteria and what is out of scope before any analysis starts Record the agreement in a scope note the sponsor confirms 02

slides.title: A request is usually one sentence, and the sentence is not the question
slides.text: How requests arrive A request is usually one sentence, and the sentence is not the question DirectorIs Awn working? The vice-rector will ask me next month. Analyst, too fastI will send you the referral numbers by Thursday. AnalystWhat will you decide once you know? "Working" could mean reaching struggling students, helping them, or costing less Each meaning needs different data, and one of them cannot be answered at all Starting the analysis before asking is the most expensive way to find that out

slides.title: Four questions turn a request into something answerable
slides.text: The conversation Four questions turn a request into something answerable The decision "What will you decide once you know?" The population "Which students, which term?" The measure "What would you count, and compared with what?" The time "When is the decision taken?" Order matters. The decision first. It tells you which answer would change what the sponsor does, and it is the purpose the law asks you for.

slides.title: Agree what a useful answer looks like before you produce one
slides.text: Success criteria Agree what a useful answer looks like before you produce one "If the answer were X, what would you do? And if it were Y?" The form: one page, a table, a number with its definition The precision that matters: to the point, or "more than half"? What would make the sponsor not believe the answer In brief B2 "One page the director can take to the council: the two rates, the groups for which they differ clearly, and the cause where it could be established."

slides.title: Write down what you will not do, while everyone still agrees
slides.text: Out of scope Write down what you will not do, while everyone still agrees The sponsor's opening sentence What was really needed Out of scope "I need the data on why engineering students are failing." Whether to add tutorial sections to two first-year courses Naming students or instructors "Is Awn working?" Extend the rule, or change its thresholds first Whether support helps: no comparison group "A nice number for the annual report." One figure with its definition, beside last year's Breakdowns with small counts Requests grow. The line "no lists of students" is the one you will point to in three weeks.

slides.title: The scope note: nine fields, one sentence each, confirmed by the sponsor
slides.text: The record The scope note: nine fields, one sentence each, confirmed by the sponsor Decision Question Population Measure Success criterion Out of scope Data Deadline Confirmed by Send it within the hour. Five lines, the question first, and one sentence you ask the sponsor to confirm by reply. An unconfirmed note is your opinion of what was agreed.

slides.title: Three habits make the six minutes work
slides.text: Technique Three habits make the six minutes work Ask, then wait One question at a time. The pause after it is where the real answer comes. Say it back "So the decision is whether to add tutorials, and you need it in three weeks." Sponsors correct a summary more easily than they answer a question. Propose the question Leave with a sentence that ends in a question mark and that data can answer. Read it aloud before you go.

slides.title: Six minutes a round: four to talk, two for feedback. Rotate the roles each round
slides.text: Role-play · three rounds Six minutes a round: four to talk, two for feedback. Rotate the roles each round One round Round 1 · brief B1 Round 2 · brief B2 Round 3 · brief B3

slides.title: Which is the best first question?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which is the best first question? A dean says: "Get me the data on why our students are failing." What does the analyst ask first? "Which fields do you want in the extract?" "Would you prefer a regression or a simple breakdown?" "Do you mean first-year students or all students?" "What do you have to decide, and by when?"

slides.title: Scope in six minutes
slides.text: Lab 3.2 · 25 min Scope in six minutes Turn a vague request into a question in a timed role-play, in threes, and write the scope note. D3_2_scoping_roleplay.ipynb Read the brief and your role card 3 min Round 1: analyst, sponsor, observer 6 min Round 2: rotate the roles 6 min Round 3: rotate the roles 6 min Write your scope note 4 min ✱ Stretch: Send the scope note as a five-line message and ask the sponsor to confirm one sentence

slides.title: Pushing back without obstructing
slides.text: Session 3 Pushing back without obstructing Refuse an unsafe request by naming the harm and the rule, not by citing policy at the sponsor Offer a lawful alternative that serves the sponsor's decision Recognise when to escalate to the data protection officer and record the agreement 03

slides.title: "A list of every student likely to fail, with names and a score, by Sunday"
slides.text: The request "A list of every student likely to fail, with names and a score, by Sunday" Why it is unsafe A named list of predicted failure is a new purpose and reaches people who do not advise the student. The score is wrong for known groups. A label that travels to deans can follow a student into grading and discipline. What she has to decide Where to put twelve new advisors, and whether the colleges act on referrals. Neither decision needs a name. The sponsor is not the villain. Dr. Ibtisam Al-Khayyat wants struggling students helped. The request is the wrong tool for a good aim.

slides.title: A refusal that works has five parts, and the alternative comes early
slides.text: The structure A refusal that works has five parts, and the alternative comes early 1 · Listen what must she decide? → 2 · Alternative what serves that decision → 3 · Harm to students, in plain words → 4 · Rule and who decides → 5 · Record what was agreed Why this order. She came with a problem. Someone who hears first how it gets solved by Sunday can listen to the reason. Someone who hears a rule first hears a refusal.

slides.title: An alternative you can show beats one you can describe
slides.text: The alternative, built An alternative you can show beats one you can describe College Referred Struggled Missed Advisors of 12 Health Sciences 479 488 165 2.7 Science 390 438 192 2.4 Arts and Humanities 317 363 181 2.0 Engineering 332 354 172 1.9 Business 306 310 153 1.7 Computing 216 238 119 1.3 Answers "where do twelve advisors go?" Every cell is 10 or more Named worklists stay with each student's advisor, as today

slides.title: Three pressures, and a reply to each that is not a rule
slides.text: What you will hear Three pressures, and a reply to each that is not a rule She says A reply that keeps the conversation "The council meets on Monday." "You will have the table for the council on Sunday. It answers where the advisors go." "Another university does this already." "Ours would wrongly list most students who attend remotely with an accommodation. I would not want your name on that list." "I am the vice-rector. I am allowed to see student data." "You are. The question is what this decision needs, and it does not need names. If you need them, the data protection officer decides, and I will take it to her today."

slides.title: Escalating is saying aloud whose decision it is
slides.text: Escalation Escalating is saying aloud whose decision it is When: the sponsor still wants named or sensitive data, a new purpose, a disclosure or a transfer To whom: the data protection officer, who monitors how the law is applied and supervises impact assessments How: three lines: what was asked and by whom, what you offered, the decision you need Copy the sponsor Escalation said aloud and copied is a service: the decision was never the analyst's, and never the sponsor's alone. Escalation behind someone's back is a complaint.

slides.title: Obstructing is as much a failure as complying
slides.text: The other failure Obstructing is as much a failure as complying Comply Send the list. The harm happens, with your name in the log. Obstruct "We cannot, it is the law." No alternative, no route. The sponsor asks someone else, who sends a worse list. Push back The decision is served by Sunday, the names stay with advisors, the record says who agreed, and the open question has an owner. The record. Asked for, will deliver, will not deliver, why, who decides more, confirmed by. What is not written down was not agreed.

slides.title: Five minutes a round: three to talk, two for the observer's five scores
slides.text: Role-play · three rounds Five minutes a round: three to talk, two for the observer's five scores One round Listen Alternative Harm Rule and who decides Record

slides.title: Which reply pushes back without obstructing?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which reply pushes back without obstructing? A dean asks for the names of students who used the counselling service, "so lecturers can go easy on them". Which reply is best? "I cannot. Counselling data is health data." "You want lecturers to support students under strain. I can give counts by department, and the service can contact lecturers for students who agree. Names would break what students were told." "I will send the list marked confidential, for department heads only." "That is a question for the data protection officer, not for me."

slides.title: Explaining limits
slides.text: Session 4 Explaining limits State what an analysis cannot show, separately from how uncertain it is Write a limits statement a non-specialist cannot misread Choose the capstone engagement and list what its pack must contain 04

slides.title: An interval tells you how sure; a limit tells you what was never measured
slides.text: Two different things An interval tells you how sure; a limit tells you what was never measured Uncertainty How far the number could move if you measured again. Awn referred 55% of struggling students, between 53% and 57%. Small, with 2,191 students. Limits What the number does not measure however often you measure: whether support helps, whether the label is right, whether the record is right, whether next term will be like this one. What goes wrong. A tight interval read as "the analysis is solid". Precision about the wrong thing is still the wrong thing.

slides.title: Six real limits, and two that only sound like limits
slides.text: The Awn evaluation Six real limits, and two that only sound like limits No test of whether support helps: no comparison group One term of one year Attendance under-recorded for remote accommodation Marks missing for bridging-year entrants "Struggled" is one definition; withdrawals can count as "ok" It describes groups, not any one student's risk Not limits "The sample is too small": 18,000 students give the overall rate to about two points. "The data is pseudonymised": a pseudonym changes who can be identified, not any rate.

slides.title: Three sentences that travel with the number
slides.text: The limits statement Three sentences that travel with the number What it shows. "In term 1, Awn referred 55% of the students who ended the term struggling (between 53% and 57%), so it missed 45% of them." What it does not show, and for whom it is worse. "The analysis did not test whether the support that follows a referral helps, and the rule is known to be less reliable for two groups: it wrongly refers many students with a remote-attendance accommodation and misses most struggling bridging-year entrants." What it must not be used for. "The result describes groups of students and must not be used to judge, rank or list any individual student."

slides.title: A statement works if it blocks the ways a hurried reader will misread the number
slides.text: Testing the statement A statement works if it blocks the ways a hurried reader will misread the number The misreading Blocked by "Awn causes students to pass." Sentence 2: support was not tested "A student Awn did not refer is safe." Sentence 1: it missed 45% "The rule works equally well for every group." Sentence 2: the two groups, named "The list of referred students can decide who repeats a course." Sentence 3: must not be used for Which side of the number. "Referred 55%" invites the second misreading. "Missed 45%" blocks it. Same fact.

slides.title: A referral is a prompt for a person, and the statement keeps it that way
slides.text: Who acts on the result A referral is a prompt for a person, and the statement keeps it that way Awn's output goes to an advisor, who talks to the student and decides People tend to favour a system's output over other evidence: the guide's automation bias "Must not be used to judge, rank or list" is the line that protects the advisor's judgement In every release The unit's policy asks for a version, a date, an approver and a line that says what the table must not be used for. The line is not decoration: it is the record that you said it.

slides.title: Which sentence belongs under the number?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which sentence belongs under the number? A slide for the University council will say "Awn referred 55% of struggling students". There is room for one more line. Which one? "95% confidence interval: 53% to 57%." "Computed on a pseudonymised extract of 18,000 students." "It missed 45%, is unreliable for two groups, and must not be used to judge individual students." "Results should be interpreted with caution."

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Day 3 Three things to keep Write it so a stranger can check it A datasheet that states the weakness, a log with a named approver, a release with a fingerprint. The decision first Ask what the sponsor has to decide. The same sentence is the scope and the lawful purpose. No, with an alternative Serve the decision, name the harm, say who decides, write it down. Then say what the number does not show.

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How the pack is scored The rubric Legal and classification decisions 25% Release tables and suppression 20% Group comparison 20% Documentation 20% Scope note 15% Every decision has a reason and an owner. "Refused" or "suppressed" without the rule, the harm and the approver is a guess, not a decision.

slides.title: Eight minutes for each defence
slides.text: Format Eight minutes for each defence 1 · The pack · 4 minutes The engagement, the sharing decision, one release table, the largest gap between groups and its likely cause. 2 · The role-play · 2 minutes A peer plays the sponsor of your brief and presses. You rescope the request. No AI assistant, no notes on screen. 3 · One fact changes · 2 minutes The assessor changes one fact of the partner's request. You revise the sharing decision aloud. Peer feedback. After each defence, everyone writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.
